title: What Is Diastasis Recti, and When Should I Get It Checked?
seoTitle: What Is Diastasis Recti? When to Get Checked
description: Diastasis recti is midline abdominal separation along the linea alba. Learn what it means, what rehab can aim for, and when a lump needs urgent care.
primaryQuestion: What is diastasis recti, and when should I get it checked?
directAnswer: Diastasis recti is a widening of the connective tissue (linea alba) between the two long rectus abdominis muscles that run down the front of the tummy. It is common in pregnancy and after birth as the growing uterus stretches the midline. It is a separation and change in that tissue—not the same as a muscle tear, and not the same as a hernia, though a hernia can coexist and needs medical review. Width or a soft dome alone does not prove you cannot function; rehab goals focus on comfort and load tolerance rather than promising a closed gap or flat abdomen.

sections.heading: What does abdominal separation mean?
paragraphs: POGP (Pelvic, Obstetric and Gynaecological Physiotherapy) describes diastasis of the rectus abdominis muscles as the two halves of the “six-pack” muscle moving apart when they can no longer stretch further around a growing pregnancy. The change can sit anywhere from under the ribcage to above the pubic bone. Hormonal softening of connective tissue and stretch from the uterus both contribute.

People often hear “open” or “closed” as if the abdomen were a zip. Tissue can be wider and still transfer load reasonably well, or narrower and still feel unstable, ache or dome when you cough, lift or sit up. Function—how the wall works with breathing, pelvic floor and daily tasks—matters more for care planning than a single fingertip count taken once at home.

A hernia is different: part of an organ or tissue pushes through a gap in the muscle wall and may form a lump. Diastasis is midline stretch and thinning of the linea alba between the rectus muscles. The two can be confused on a selfie; only a clinician can sort them. Physiotherapy does not diagnose hernia.

sections.heading: What might you notice—and what are fair rehab goals?
paragraphs: Common observations include a soft midline when you lie down, a ridge or dome when you sit up, or a tummy that still looks pregnant months after birth. Some people notice discomfort with lifting or long standing; others mainly notice how clothes sit. Leakage or pelvic heaviness can travel with abdominal-wall changes but are not proof of diastasis—those belong in a wider pelvic-health conversation.

Reasonable goals include moving and lifting with more comfort, reducing bothersome doming during the tasks that matter to you, and rebuilding graded strength. Closing a gap to a fixed finger width or guaranteeing a flat abdomen is not a fair promise. Time, load and coaching can help tissue remodel and strategy improve; outcomes still vary.

Avoid framing everyday technique as morally “good” or “wrong.” Rolling to the side to get out of bed, keeping loads close, and building walking before hard abdominal drills are practical load choices—not character judgements. Our page on what a self-check can tell you covers observation limits without repeating the full definition here.

sections.heading: What will a physiotherapist assess?
paragraphs: Dr. Zalak Shah (PT) reviews your birth and activity history, then looks at breathing, how the abdominal wall behaves in positions that match your life, and pelvic-floor coordination where relevant. Findings guide graded loading—often pressure management and everyday tasks first—rather than a blanket ban on all core work or an immediate jump to advanced Pilates.

She assesses movement and function; she does not diagnose hernia or other surgical conditions. If a lump, pain pattern or digestive symptoms raise medical concern, she will direct you to medical review. Medical gynaecology or surgical questions at Women’s Health Duo sit with Dr. Charmi Shah.

sections.heading: When is medical or urgent care needed?
paragraphs: Book a timely medical review for a persistent unexplained bulge, pain at rest, or any suspicion of hernia. Seek urgent or emergency care for an acutely painful, firm lump that will not go back in, especially with vomiting, severe tummy pain, or inability to pass wind or stool. UK NHS hernia guidance treats painful hernia symptoms with sickness, constipation or confusion as reasons to get urgent help—possible strangulation is a medical emergency, not a physiotherapy scheduling question.
Routine physiotherapy booking fits when you mainly want help with load tolerance, breathing and bracing strategies, or return to activity after medical concerns are addressed or cleared.

faqs.question: Is diastasis recti a torn muscle?
faqs.answer: No. It describes the rectus muscles moving apart as the midline connective tissue widens and thins. That is different from a tear through muscle fibres and different from a hernia, where tissue pushes through a defect in the wall.

faqs.question: Does a wider gap always mean worse function?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily. Width is only one observation. How the wall tensions during real tasks, symptoms such as pain or leakage, and your goals matter more for planning rehab than a single resting measurement.

sourcesChecked.title: Tummy muscle separation (DRAM) in pregnancy
sourcesChecked.recommendation: Defines DRAM as rectus halves moving apart with pregnancy stretch; lists doming, gap feeling, discomfort; advises graded core work and physio referral.
sourcesChecked.passage: This is where the two halves of one of the tummy muscles called the rectus abdominus, or the ‘six pack’ muscle, move apart once they are not able to stretch any more.
sourcesChecked.limitations: UK patient leaflet; symptom lists are not diagnostic criteria

sourcesChecked.title: Hernia
sourcesChecked.recommendation: Hernia is organ/tissue through muscle gap; pain around hernia with nausea/vomiting warrants urgent advice pathway.
sourcesChecked.passage: A hernia is where part of an internal organ, such as your bowel, pushes through a gap or weak area in the muscle that keeps your organs in place.
sourcesChecked.limitations: General hernia overview; not specific to postpartum diastasis

sourcesChecked.title: Umbilical hernia
sourcesChecked.recommendation: Strangulated hernia (blocked blood supply) is a medical emergency; call emergency services for severe pain, vomiting, colour change, inability to pass wind/stool.
sourcesChecked.passage: The most serious complication of an umbilical hernia is when the blood supply to the bowel becomes blocked (strangulated hernia). This is a medical emergency
sourcesChecked.limitations: Umbilical-hernia page; apply carefully when counselling midline lumps

openQuestions: Clinician review of escalation wording: acutely painful, firm lump that will not reduce, especially with vomiting → urgent care for possible strangulated hernia—confirm preferred patient-facing phrasing for Indian emergency pathways.
